finalAnswer: Compute $B_{ij}=G_{ij}\oplus G_{i1}\oplus G_{1j}\oplus G_{11}$ for $i,j>1$. A valid cow corresponds to $B$ being exactly the whole interior block, one full interior column, one full interior row, or one interior cell. Check these cases in that order for the smallest row and column; otherwise print `-1`.
shortExplanation: The four-corner XOR is unchanged by every whole-row or whole-column flip, and it is zero precisely when the grid can be made uniform. Flipping one cow toggles one of four known patterns in this invariant, so its position can be determined without simulating all possible shout sequences.
detailedSteps: **Find an invariant that captures all shout sequences.** Encode the two directions by $0$ and $1$. For each interior position, $B_{ij}=G_{ij}\oplus G_{i1}\oplus G_{1j}\oplus G_{11}$. A row or column flip changes zero or two of these terms, so it cannot change $B$. Any uniform grid has $B=0$.

**Prove zero is also sufficient.** Flip each row $i$ according to its first entry $G_{i1}$, making the first column zero. Then flip column $j$ according to $G_{1j}\oplus G_{11}$, making the first row zero. The remaining interior entries are exactly $B$. Thus $B=0$ characterizes all grids that can be made uniform, including either common facing direction.

**Determine the effect of flipping a single cow.** An interior cow toggles just one invariant entry. A cow in the first row but outside the corner toggles its entire interior column. A cow in the first column but outside the corner toggles its entire interior row. The upper-left cow toggles the whole $(N-1)\times(N-1)$ interior block. The corrected grid can be made uniform exactly when the current $B$ equals that cow’s toggle pattern.

**Match patterns and obey the requested tie rule.** Count interior ones and each row and column total. If every interior entry is one, the corner $(1,1)$ works and is earliest. Otherwise a full column containing all $N-1$ ones gives $(1,j)$, before any later row. A full row containing all $N-1$ ones gives $(i,1)$. A single interior one gives its own position. If none applies, no single cow has the required pattern, so print `-1`.

**Handle the smallest dimension and the negative branch.** When $N=2$, all four toggle patterns coincide with the one-entry interior; the first all-ones check correctly chooses $(1,1)$ among the four candidates. A zero invariant has no valid single-cow correction for $N\geq2$, because every toggle pattern is nonzero. This follows the output’s explicit no-such-cow branch as well as the narrative’s one-error setting.

**Bound the work.** Reading and scanning the grid costs $O(N^2)$ time. The input grid uses $O(N^2)$ space and the extra counters use $O(N)$; no exponential operation-sequence search is needed. Counts are below $10^6$. Preserve the output distinction between one row-column pair and the single value `-1`.
keyIdeas: A four-corner XOR removes both row and column freedoms.
A complete invariant needs a converse construction, not only a necessary condition.
Classifying a single error by its effect on the invariant resolves the coordinate and the lexicographic tie.
commonMistakes: Checking only the number of ones, without verifying the complete row or column shape.
Ignoring the $N=2$ overlap between pattern types and returning a later coordinate.
Finding any correctable cow instead of the smallest row and then smallest column.
Assuming a zero invariant has a single-cow solution rather than checking the defined negative branch.

For small grids, enumerate actual row/column flip masks and try every single-cell flip against their orbit. This independent physical check uses no invariant formula and is exponential.
difficultyNotes: The main step is proving that the invariant fully characterizes uniformizability. The negative branch is explicitly specified by the output; tests for that branch are kept separate from the narrative’s positive one-error examples.

finalAnswer: Find any intersecting pair using an exact $O(N\log N)$ sweep. The source’s one-removal guarantee restricts the answer to that pair. Check each candidate against all other segments; if both can be removed, output the smaller original index.
shortExplanation: Any deletion that fixes all intersections must delete one endpoint of an already-found conflict. An exact sweep supplies that conflict efficiently, including vertical segments, collinear overlap and closed contacts. The one-removal promise then turns a general geometric problem into two candidate checks.
detailedSteps: **Test closed intersections with integer geometry.** Reject disjoint coordinate bounding boxes. Otherwise compute orientation signs for each pair of endpoints against the other segment’s supporting line. Both pairs must have opposite signs or include zero. For nonparallel lines these conditions place the intersection within both segments; for collinear lines the bounding-box overlap is the projected overlap. Endpoint-to-interior contact counts as an intersection even though all source endpoints are globally distinct.

**Maintain nonvertical segments in their exact vertical order.** Normalize a sloped segment to left endpoint $(x_\ell,y_\ell)$ and right endpoint $(x_r,y_r)$, with $d=x_r-x_\ell>0$. At sweep coordinate $X$, its height is the rational value $[y_\ell d+(y_r-y_\ell)(X-x_\ell)]/d$. Cross-multiply to compare heights exactly; the implementation uses signed 128-bit arithmetic because comparison products can be of order $10^{27}$. There is no floating-point tolerance.

**Use a balanced tree whose stored sequence stays valid.** The original implementation uses an explicit AVL tree with source-index handles. Insert by current exact height; remove by the stored handle. Height-balanced rotations preserve the in-order sequence and give worst-case logarithmic operations. Vertical segments are handled separately, so no zero denominator enters the height comparison.

**Check every newly adjacent pair.** After inserting a nonvertical segment, test it against its predecessor and successor using their full closed segments, even if an intersection would occur later. After removing a segment, test the predecessor and successor that become neighbors. Return as soon as any such pair intersects.

**Prove the sweep cannot miss an intersection.** Before the first physical intersection, active vertical order cannot change. Just before an earliest intersection, some intersecting pair is adjacent in that order; if several segments meet at the same point, an adjacent pair among them still exists. That pair became adjacent at an insertion or removal event no later than the intersection, where the full-segment test would already have found it. Thus execution cannot pass an undetected order change, and every height search remains valid until a pair is returned.

**Process equal-coordinate events as closed geometry.** At a shared $x$ coordinate, insert all nonvertical starts, then check vertical segments, then remove all nonvertical ends. This keeps both starting and ending segments present during contact checks. For a vertical segment with height interval $[u,v]$, find the first active nonvertical height at least $u$ and test whether it is at most $v$. For vertical-vertical intersections, sort their lower endpoints and test each against the largest preceding upper endpoint. Inclusive comparisons handle contacts and collinear overlap.

**Reduce the removal decision using the actual source promise.** Suppose the found pair is $(a,b)$. Any successful removal must be $a$ or $b$, since deleting another segment leaves their intersection. If $a$ also intersects some segment other than $b$, deleting $b$ fails, and the promised successful deletion must be $a$. The symmetric case chooses $b$. Both extra-conflict flags cannot occur on a promised input. If neither occurs, the promise rules out any conflict outside this pair, so both deletions work and the smaller original index is correct.

**Verify complexity and scope.** Sorting events and vertical groups, plus balanced-tree operations, costs $O(N\log N)$ time; the final candidate comparisons cost $O(N)$. Storage is $O(N)$. Globally distinct endpoints exclude zero-length segments and repeated endpoints, but do not exclude verticals, parallelism, collinearity or an endpoint on another segment’s interior. The original solver uses the printed at-least-one-intersection and one-successful-removal guarantees.
keyIdeas: One known conflict limits any successful single deletion to two segment indices.
An exact sweep checks new neighbors before an unnoticed crossing could invalidate their order.
Closed event phases and vertical interval queries cover the degenerate cases.
Wide rational comparisons protect ordering, which requires more precision than merely storing input coordinates.
commonMistakes: Using a quadratic all-pairs search at the full $10^5$-segment limit.
Ignoring vertical lines, collinear overlap or endpoint-to-interior contacts.
Relying on floating-point height comparisons or multiplying 32-bit coordinate differences.
Allowing active order to change silently without detecting the crossing.
Choosing any candidate or assuming a general collection always admits a single deletion; the guarantee and earliest-index tie are essential.
alternativeMethods: For small collections, solve each pair of supporting-line parameters using exact rational arithmetic, handle parallel collinear intervals, and then enumerate every possible deletion. This independently verifies closed intersections and the earliest answer in $O(N^2)$ time.

finalAnswer: For every connected moo network, compute $P=2[(x_{\max}-x_{\min})+(y_{\max}-y_{\min})]$. Print the minimum $P$ over all networks, allowing either span to be zero.
shortExplanation: Any axis-parallel rectangle enclosing a network must cover its full horizontal and vertical coordinate ranges. Its closed bounding rectangle attains those required spans, so it has the least perimeter for that network. Choose the least such perimeter among the connected components.
detailedSteps: **Identify whole networks.** Treat cows as graph vertices and moo connections as undirected edges. A network is a connected component, not one individual edge. Traverse each component iteratively and collect its smallest and largest $x$ and $y$ coordinates. Cycles do not change the component definition.

**Prove a lower bound for any enclosing fence.** If a component has horizontal extremes $x_{\min},x_{\max}$, any enclosing axis-parallel rectangle must have width at least $x_{\max}-x_{\min}$. Its height must likewise be at least $y_{\max}-y_{\min}$. Therefore its perimeter is at least twice the sum of those spans.

**Attain the bound, including zero dimensions.** The component’s closed bounding rectangle has exactly these spans and contains every cow, including those on its boundary. A horizontal or vertical network can use zero height or width, which the source explicitly permits. Other cows may lie inside too; the requirement is to contain at least one whole network, not to isolate it from every other cow.

**Choose the globally optimal component.** Every feasible fence encloses some complete component, so its perimeter is at least that component’s bound and hence at least the smallest bound over all components. The bounding rectangle of the minimizing component attains that global minimum.

**Respect the printed input and bound the work.** All cow points are distinct, every cow has a moo connection, no connection is repeated, and the source has the strict edge bound $M<10^5$. Iterative traversal costs $O(N+M)$ time and space. The largest possible perimeter under coordinate bound $10^8$ is $4\cdot10^8$, so the implementation’s `long long` is conservative; no recursion through $10^5$ cows is required.
keyIdeas: Connectedness determines which cows must be enclosed together.
Coordinate extremes give both a necessary lower bound and an attaining rectangle.
Optimizing at least one complete component requires a minimum across component bounds.
commonMistakes: Using the bounding box of the entire farm instead of the best single network.
Considering only directly connected pairs and omitting the rest of their component.
Adding width or height to avoid zero-area rectangles when the source explicitly allows zero dimensions.
Treating the source’s strict $M<10^5$ bound as inclusive or generating isolated cows despite their connection guarantee.
alternativeMethods: A disjoint-set structure can build the components, then aggregate four coordinate extremes at their representatives.

For a small geometric oracle, enumerate closed rectangles with sides at input coordinates and directly test whether each contains a whole network. This checks enclosure and perimeter without using the extrema accumulator.
